steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper asking whether one large cross-embodiment policy can benefit from training on both navigation and manipulation data. Motivate why transfer between the two domains might work and summarize what we found.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Foundation models and large robot datasets; prior work limited to similar embodiments
- Our question: transfer across navigation and manipulation
- Why transfer could work: shared sensorimotor principles
- What we show in this paper

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - large-scale foundation models: diverse data -> sample efficiency, generalization, transfer to novel domains
  - robotics: acceleration in collecting / consolidating large datasets for the same benefits
  - data spans scenes, observations, viewpoints, tasks, embodiments; domains: manipulation, navigation, autonomous driving, others
  - but prior work restricted to similar embodiments, e.g. arms with parallel jaw grippers
  - most successful foundation models trained on highly heterogeneous data (web text)
  - question: how much embodiment diversity for "generalist" robot policies?
- Our setting
  - heterogeneous embodiments; can large policies benefit from data across navigation and manipulation?
  - avoids recollecting data present in one domain but not the other
  - navigation data -> spatial relationships between poses for manipulators
  - manipulation data -> object-centric reasoning for navigators
  - crucial for mobile manipulators (base + arm both approach objects)
- Why positive transfer?
  - domains differ in hardware, observations, action representations, but share sensorimotor principles
  - both need understanding of collisions and geometry
  - both need visual servoing: manipulation = end-effector vs target object; navigation = current location vs goal from images
  - wrist-mounted camera vs forward-facing camera: same equivariance between pose changes and observations ("left" in image)
- Contributions
  - first results (to our knowledge): large-scale policy trained jointly on navigation + manipulation data from many robots; controls arms, drones, quadrupeds, mobile bases, mobile manipulators
  - co-trained policy: 20% higher success than manipulation-only
  - 5-7% improvement over navigation-only on 4 different robots
  - which datasets most useful for manipulation; navigation data -> embeddings more informative of distance to goal in novel manipulation environments
  - generalizes to two new robots (mobile manipulator, quadrotor) with no embodiment-specific data
  - training method / architecture from prior techniques; empirical findings are the novel contribution

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale foundation models in machine learning have made it possible to use diverse datasets to improve sample efficiency and generalization, and to help transfer to novel domains. In robotics, recent years have seen an acceleration in collecting and consolidating large-scale datasets, in the hope of getting similar benefits. These datasets have demonstrations that span many scenes, observations, viewpoints, tasks, and embodiments, in a wide range of robotics domains like manipulation, navigation, autonomous driving, and others. However, these prior works usually restrict what they study to sets of similar embodiments, for example arms with parallel jaw grippers. On the other hand, the most successful large-scale foundation models are usually trained on very heterogeneous data, such as large text corpora mined from the web. So the question is: how much embodiment diversity can we include when we train broadly capable "generalist" robot policies?

We study this question for heterogeneous embodiments, and we want to understand whether large-scale policies can benefit from data across navigation and manipulation. If this transfer of knowledge works, it removes the need to recollect datasets that contain information that is present in one domain but not in the other. For example, navigation data can help manipulators understand spatial relationships between different poses. In the same way, manipulation data can help navigators with object-centric reasoning. This is especially important for mobile manipulators, which need both the mobile base and the robotic arm to approach some objects.

- Why positive transfer?
  - domains differ (hardware, observations, action representations) but share sensorimotor principles
  - collisions and geometry in both
  - visual servoing in both: end-effector vs target object / current location vs goal from images
  - wrist-mounted vs forward-facing camera: same equivariance between pose changes and observations
- Contributions
  - first large-scale policy jointly trained on navigation + manipulation from many robots; controls arms, drones, quadrupeds, mobile bases, mobile manipulators
  - 20% higher success than manipulation-only; 5-7% over navigation-only on 4 robots
  - most useful datasets for manipulation; navigation data -> embeddings more informative of distance to goal
  - generalizes to mobile manipulator and quadrotor without their data
  - methods from prior work, findings are the novel part

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large-scale foundation models in machine learning have made it possible to use diverse datasets to improve sample efficiency and generalization, and to help transfer to novel domains. In robotics, recent years have seen an acceleration in collecting and consolidating large-scale datasets, in the hope of getting similar benefits. These datasets have demonstrations that span many scenes, observations, viewpoints, tasks, and embodiments, in a wide range of robotics domains like manipulation, navigation, autonomous driving, and others. However, these prior works usually restrict what they study to sets of similar embodiments, for example arms with parallel jaw grippers. On the other hand, the most successful large-scale foundation models are usually trained on very heterogeneous data, such as large text corpora mined from the web. So the question is: how much embodiment diversity can we include when we train broadly capable "generalist" robot policies?

We study this question for heterogeneous embodiments, and we want to understand whether large-scale policies can benefit from data across navigation and manipulation. If this transfer of knowledge works, it removes the need to recollect datasets that contain information that is present in one domain but not in the other. For example, navigation data can help manipulators understand spatial relationships between different poses. In the same way, manipulation data can help navigators with object-centric reasoning. This is especially important for mobile manipulators, which need both the mobile base and the robotic arm to approach some objects.

Why would we expect positive transfer between navigation and manipulation? The two domains seem very different in hardware, observations, and action representations, but they have many similar sensorimotor principles. For example, in both domains the learned robot policy needs to understand collisions and geometry. Both domains also need the agent to do some kind of visual servoing. In manipulation, the robot looks at its observation to figure out where its end-effector is relative to a target object, and then it moves towards it. In visual navigation it is similar: the robot looks at the spatial relationship between its current location and the goal, which it infers from image observations, and decides how to move toward the goal. If the manipulation task uses a wrist-mounted camera and the navigation task uses a forward-facing camera, then both embodiments have the same equivariance between pose changes and camera observations, i.e. moving "left" with respect to the image changes the observations in egocentric manipulation and in navigation in a similar way.

In this paper we empirically investigate the benefits of including navigation data for robotic manipulation, and also the other way around. To our knowledge, we present the first results that show a large-scale policy trained jointly on navigation and manipulation data from many different robots, and we show that this policy can control robotic arms, drones, quadrupeds, mobile bases, and mobile manipulators. We then show that a co-trained policy gets a 20% higher success rate than a manipulation-only policy. Interestingly, the same co-trained policy also gets a 5-7% improvement over a navigation-only policy on 4 different robots. This suggests that robotic agents can benefit from data collected across very different embodiments. We then look at which datasets are the most useful for manipulation, and we show that navigation data helps the policy learn embeddings that are more informative of the distance to the goal in novel manipulation environments. Finally we show that our policy can generalize to two new robots, a mobile manipulator and a quadrotor, without any data specific to these embodiments. The training methodology and model architecture are based on prior techniques, but the empirical findings are a novel contribution of our work, and they show for the first time that navigation data can give quantifiable benefits for robotic manipulation in the cross-embodied policy learning setting.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The advent of large-scale foundation models in machine learning has made it possible to harness diverse datasets to enhance sample efficiency, improve generalization, and facilitate transfer to novel domains [1]. Recent years in robotics have seen an acceleration in the collection and consolidation of large-scale datasets in the hope of obtaining similar benefits. These datasets contain demonstrations spanning many scenes, observations, viewpoints, tasks, and embodiments in a wide range of robotics domains such as manipulation [2,3,4], navigation [5,6], autonomous driving [7], and others [8]. However, these prior works typically restrict their investigations to sets of similar embodiments – e.g., arms with parallel jaw grippers. In contrast, the most successful large-scale foundation models are typically trained on highly heterogeneous data, such as large text corpora mined from the web. This raises the question: what degree of embodiment diversity can we include when training broadly capable "generalist" robot policies?

We study this problem in the context of heterogeneous embodiments, aiming to understand whether large-scale policies can benefit from data across navigation and manipulation. Enabling this transfer of knowledge can remove the need to recollect datasets containing information that is present in one domain but not the other. For example, navigation data can help manipulators understand spatial relationships between different poses, and manipulation data can similarly help navigators with object-centric reasoning. This is particularly important for mobile manipulators, which need both the mobile base and the robotic arm to approach certain objects.

Why might we hope for positive transfer across navigation and manipulation? Although these domains seem to differ significantly in terms of hardware, observations, and action representations, they share many sensorimotor principles. For example, both domains require the learned robot policy to understand collisions and geometry. Both domains also require the agent to perform some form of visual servoing. In manipulation, the robot analyzes its observation to determine the position of its end-effector relative to a target object, and then moves towards it. Similarly, in visual navigation, the robot examines the spatial relationship between its current location and the goal, as inferred from image observations, and determines how to move toward the goal. If the manipulation task uses a wrist-mounted camera and the navigation task uses a forward-facing camera, both embodiments have the same equivariance between pose changes and camera observations – i.e., moving "left" with respect to the image transforms the observations in egocentric manipulation and navigation in a similar way.

In this paper, we empirically investigate the benefits of including navigation data for robotic manipulation, and vice versa. We present, to our knowledge, the first results showing a large-scale policy trained jointly on navigation and manipulation data from many different robots, and show that such a policy can control robotic arms, drones, quadrupeds, mobile bases, and mobile manipulators. We then demonstrate that a co-trained policy achieves a 20% higher success rate than a manipulation-only policy. Interestingly, the same co-trained policy achieves a 5-7% improvement over a navigation-only policy on 4 different robots. This suggests that robotic agents can benefit from data collected across significantly different embodiments. We then characterize which datasets are most useful for manipulation and show that navigation data helps the policy learn embeddings that are more informative of distance to the goal in novel manipulation environments. Finally, we show that our policy can generalize to two new robots, a mobile manipulator and a quadrotor, without any data specific to these embodiments. While the training methodology and model architecture are based on prior techniques, the empirical findings are a novel contribution of our work, demonstrating for the first time that navigation data can provide quantifiable benefits for robotic manipulation in the cross-embodied policy learning setting.
